question: Why does metal feel colder than wood?
script: Touch a metal handle and a wooden surface in the same room. The metal often feels colder even when both started at almost the same temperature. Your skin is warmer than the room, so thermal energy flows from your hand into both materials. The difference is speed. Metals usually have much higher thermal conductivity than wood, so they carry energy away from the contact point quickly. Your skin cools faster, and your nerves interpret that faster cooling as a colder sensation. Wood moves heat much more slowly, so the tiny patch under your hand warms up and the heat flow soon decreases. This means touch is not a perfect thermometer. What you feel depends strongly on the rate of heat transfer, not just the object’s starting temperature. The metal is not secretly colder; it is simply much better at moving thermal energy away from your skin.
beats: Both can start at the same temperature
Energy flows out of your skin
